title: Message Queues & Event-Driven Architecture
intro: Message queues decouple distributed producers and consumers, smoothing out spiky workloads, absorbing traffic surges, and guaranteeing reliable asynchronous processing.
objectives: Contrast point-to-point queues (RabbitMQ, SQS) with append-only distributed event logs (Kafka).
Formulate message delivery guarantees: At-Least-Once, At-Most-Once, and Exactly-Once (Idempotency).
Implement Dead Letter Queues (DLQ) and exponential retry policies.
body:
### Why Asynchronous Messaging Matters
Synchronous HTTP request-reply chains couple services together: if service $C$ is slow or down, services $A$ and $B$ block, exhausting worker threads and causing cascading outages. Message queues decouple this pipeline:
- **Buffering (Leaky Bucket)**: Queue absorbs a 10x traffic spike while background workers consume at a steady, sustainable pace.
- **Temporal Decoupling**: Producers can emit messages even if consumer workers are temporarily offline for deployment.
- **Dead Letter Queue (DLQ)**: Poison pill messages that fail repeatedly after max retries are quarantined for developer inspection without clogging the main queue.
keyIdea: Decouple synchronous HTTP chains with asynchronous queues. Treat delivery as 'At-Least-Once' and make all consumer handlers idempotent.

concepts.title: Backpressure
concepts.body: Signaling producers to slow down when downstream consumer queues exceed memory or latency thresholds.

concepts.title: Poison Pill Messages
concepts.body: Malformed messages that crash consumer processes upon receipt, requiring quarantine via DLQs.

examples: AWS SQS triggering Lambda workers for background video transcode jobs.

quiz.prompt: What is the purpose of a Dead Letter Queue (DLQ)?
options: To isolate unprocessable messages after repeated retries without halting the pipeline
To replicate messages across AWS regions
quiz.explanation: A DLQ captures poison pill messages that fail processing repeatedly, allowing normal traffic to continue unblocked.
